structured_output.hypothesis: If the claim holds, 100-year-smoothed ring-width chronologies of Arizona ponderosa (yellow) pine covering about AD 1417-1917 will show a single dominant spectral peak at a period of 150 ± 10 years. The peak will exceed a red-noise (AR1) 95% null and will recur in most independent Arizona chronologies.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Take all ITRDB Arizona Pinus ponderosa chronologies that cover AD 1417-1917 with at least 5 trees per year, and a regional composite built from them. Detrend conservatively, apply a 100-year smoother, and compute multitaper (NW=2) and Lomb-Scargle spectra. PASS requires all three of the following. (a) The regional composite has its largest spectral peak within 140-160 years, and that peak exceeds the 95% AR1 red-noise confidence level (Monte Carlo, 1000 surrogates). (b) At least 60% of the individual qualifying chronologies have a significant (p<0.05) peak within 140-160 years. (c) The peak is still within 140-160 years and still significant when the record is split and the peak is re-estimated on the 1417-1917 window with 50-year-shifted start and end dates.
structured_output.fail_criterion: FAIL if any of the following holds. (a) The composite's strongest peak lies outside 140-160 years. (b) The composite's peak within 140-160 years does not exceed the AR1 95% level. (c) Fewer than 40% of individual chronologies show a significant peak in 140-160 years. (d) The peak period shifts by more than 20 years under the 50-year window shifts. Results between the PASS and FAIL thresholds are reported as inconclusive and count as not confirmed.
structured_output.interpretation: 'Yellow pine' is read as Pinus ponderosa. 'Century-smoothed annual ring widths' is read as standardized ring-width indices passed through a 100-year low-pass filter. 'Regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years' is read as a statistically significant narrow-band spectral peak at 150 ± 10 years, not merely a visual undulation. Over 500 years that is only about 3.3 cycles, so spectral resolution is limited, and smoothing and detrending can themselves create spurious low-frequency peaks. That is why a red-noise null is required. 'Climate fluctuated' is read as a regional signal shared across sites, tested by how many chronologies show the peak. The 'moisture rather than temperature' part is not tested, because the plan tests the periodicity only. Modern dendroclimatology treats ring width in Arizona pines as chiefly a precipitation and drought proxy, and this plan makes no attempt to confirm that.

dataset.name: International Tree-Ring Data Bank (ITRDB)
dataset.publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) World Data Service for Paleoclimatology
dataset.why_it_fits: The ITRDB holds many public ring-width measurement files (.rwl) and standardized chronologies (.crn) for Arizona Pinus ponderosa sites, and many of them span the last 500 years. Fields used are species code (PIPO), state (Arizona), site latitude and longitude, year, ring-width measurement or chronology index, and sample depth. These allow the smoothing, spectral and red-noise tests specified above.
